title: Advanced usage of gipsDA
text: Scaling may useful predictors measured different scales. However, scaling done carefully: center scale estimated training data applied new data. fit model scaled data. Scaling always necessary. depends whether original variables already comparable whether scaling meaningful application.
code: x_train <- train[, 1:4] x_test <- test[, 1:4]  train_center <- vapply(x_train, mean, numeric(1)) train_scale <- vapply(x_train, sd, numeric(1))  train_scaled <- train test_scaled <- test  train_scaled[, 1:4] <- scale(   x_train,   center = train_center,   scale = train_scale )  test_scaled[, 1:4] <- scale(   x_test,   center = train_center,   scale = train_scale ) fit_scaled <- gipslda(Species ~ ., data = train_scaled) pred_scaled <- predict(fit_scaled, test_scaled)  mean(pred_scaled$class == test_scaled$Species) #> [1] 0.9777778

title: Advanced usage of gipsDA
text: package provides three main classifiers. Fit three models data. Compare test-set accuracy.
code: lda_fit <- gipslda(Species ~ ., data = train) qda_fit <- gipsqda(Species ~ ., data = train) joint_qda_fit <- gipsmultqda(Species ~ ., data = train) lda_pred <- predict(lda_fit, test) qda_pred <- predict(qda_fit, test) joint_qda_pred <- predict(joint_qda_fit, test)  c(   gipslda = mean(lda_pred$class == test$Species),   gipsqda = mean(qda_pred$class == test$Species),   gipsmultqda = mean(joint_qda_pred$class == test$Species) ) #>     gipslda     gipsqda gipsmultqda  #>   0.9777778   0.9777778   1.0000000

text: weighted_avg argument specific gipslda(). controls pooled covariance matrix constructed gips projection applied. Let: KK number classes, nkn_k number observations class kk, n=∑k=1Knkn = \sum_{k=1}^{K} n_k total number observations, SkS_k sample covariance matrix class kk. weighted_avg = FALSE, gipslda() uses classic pooled covariance estimator: Sclassic=1n−K∑k=1K(nk−1)Sk. S_{\mathrm{classic}} = \frac{1}{n - K} \sum_{k = 1}^{K} (n_k - 1) S_k. weighted_avg = TRUE, gipslda() uses: Sweighted=1n∑k=1KnkSk. S_{\mathrm{weighted}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k = 1}^{K} n_k S_k. Fit variants. Compare predictions. two variants can behave differently class sizes imbalanced class-specific covariance estimates differ substantially.
